title: Chapter XLV

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth and Mrs. Gardiner visit Pemberley. Caroline Bingley tries to provoke Elizabeth by mentioning the militia (Wickham), embarrassing Georgiana. Darcy defends Elizabeth, calling her one of the handsomest women he knows.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLV,” how does Austen show jealousy at Pemberley? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLV develops the idea of jealousy at Pemberley. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLV to complicate the reader's understanding of jealousy at Pemberley. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of jealousy at Pemberley responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of jealousy at Pemberley. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Why does Caroline's attack backfire? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include predominate, peaches, nettled, pyramids, chestnuts. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Darcy, by the feelings which prevailed on his entering the room; and then, though but a moment before she had believed her wishes to predominate, she began to regret that he came.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: To be superior in number, strength, influence, or authority.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Polite visits were also contests of status and wit. Now, why does this chapter matter? Caroline's spite backfires, revealing Darcy's devotion. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Plot.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
